destinations.photo: Lisbon · Alfama rooftops at golden hour

honest.trip: Easy to land in and walkable, but the hills and old trams mean slow crosstown trips. August is hot and tourist-packed.
honest.nomad: A genuine nomad hub with great cafés and a big community — which means rents have climbed fast and the best flats go in days.
honest.move: Sunny, safe and welcoming, with a clear residency path. Bureaucracy is slow and finding long-term housing takes patience.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU, CA & AU passports enter Schengen visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day window.

nomad.headline: Digital Nomad Visa (D8)
nomad.body: For stays over 90 days. Show remote income of roughly €3,280/mo. Renewable, and counts toward residency.

move.headline: Residence permit (D7 / D8)
move.body: Apply from a long-stay visa, then a residence permit. Permanent residency possible after 5 years.

destinations.photo: Mexico City · leafy Roma Norte streets

honest.trip: Huge, vibrant and great value, but the scale means long taxi rides and altitude can leave you breathless for a day or two.
honest.nomad: Incredible food, culture and a fast-growing remote scene. Roma & Condesa are lovely but rents there now rival European cities.
honest.move: Warm people and a low cost of living, but you'll want functional Spanish and patience for paperwork to truly settle.

trip.headline: Visa-free, up to 180 days
trip.body: Many nationalities enter as a tourist for a stay set on arrival — commonly up to 180 days.

nomad.headline: Tourist entry covers it
nomad.body: No dedicated nomad visa, but the generous tourist entry comfortably covers a 1–3 month stint.

move.headline: Temporary Resident Visa
move.body: Apply at a consulate with proof of income or savings. Valid 1–4 years and leads to permanent residency.

destinations.photo: Bangkok · Chao Phraya river at dusk

honest.trip: Cheap, fast and endlessly convenient — but heat, humidity and traffic are real. Get a hotel near a BTS Skytrain stop.
honest.nomad: Unbeatable value with modern condos and cafés everywhere. Air quality dips in the burning season (Feb–Apr).
honest.move: Comfortable and affordable for years, though long-term visas need planning and property ownership rules are strict.

trip.headline: Visa-exemption on arrival
trip.body: Many passports get a 30–60 day visa-exempt stay on entry, extendable once at an immigration office.

nomad.headline: Destination Thailand Visa
nomad.body: The DTV allows 180 days per entry over a 5-year multi-entry validity — built for remote workers.

move.headline: Long-Term Resident visa
move.body: The LTR visa offers up to 10 years for qualifying professionals, retirees and high earners.

honest.trip: Astonishing value and famously easy entry, but it's smaller and quieter than the big hubs — charming, not buzzing.
honest.nomad: One of the simplest places in the world to base yourself, with cheap flats and fast wifi. English is less common day-to-day.
honest.move: Very low cost of living and light bureaucracy, though it's further from family back home and winters are grey.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 1 year
trip.body: Around 95 nationalities can enter and stay visa-free for a full 365 days — one of the most generous policies anywhere.

nomad.headline: Remotely from Georgia
nomad.body: A simple program for remote workers and freelancers to stay long-term, on top of the 1-year visa-free entry.

move.headline: Residence permits
move.body: Work, study and investment residence permits are straightforward, with a path to permanent residency.

destinations.photo: Berlin · Spree riverside & TV tower skyline

honest.trip: Endlessly walkable with world-class museums and nightlife, but grey winters and patchy English at counters can catch first-timers off guard.
honest.nomad: A huge, established freelancer scene with cheap-by-European-standards rent — though the famous bureaucracy (Anmeldung, Bürgeramt queues) tests everyone's patience.
honest.move: Affordable, green and tolerant, with strong tenant protections. Apartment hunting is genuinely competitive and German fluency unlocks far more.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, CA & AU passports enter Schengen visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day window.

nomad.headline: Freelance visa (Freiberufler)
nomad.body: Self-employed professionals can apply for a freelance residence permit with proof of clients and income.

move.headline: Residence permit + Anmeldung
move.body: Register your address (Anmeldung) within 14 days, then apply for a residence permit. PR possible after 5 years.

destinations.photo: Buenos Aires · Palermo Soho cafés and jacarandas

honest.trip: Gorgeous European-style architecture and unbeatable steak, but inflation means prices shift fast and ATMs often run dry.
honest.nomad: A buzzing café and coworking culture with some of the best value left in the Americas — though the peso's swings make budgeting a moving target.
honest.move: Warm, cultured and welcoming, with relatively easy residency, but the economy's volatility affects everyday banking and savings.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU, CA & AU passports enter visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days.

nomad.headline: Digital Nomad Visa
nomad.body: A renewable visa for remote workers earning foreign income, valid up to 180 days per stay.

move.headline: Rentista / residency visa
move.body: Show steady passive or foreign income to qualify for temporary residency, renewable toward permanent status.

honest.trip: Immaculately run and endlessly fascinating, but it's expensive by Asian standards and queues/etiquette norms take adjusting to.
honest.nomad: Fast, reliable everything and a small but growing remote-work scene — though English is limited and short-term flexible leases are scarce.
honest.move: Safe, efficient and high quality of life, but visa sponsorship usually needs a local employer and the language barrier is real for daily life.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU, CA & AU passports enter visa-free for short tourism or business stays.

nomad.headline: Digital Nomad Visa
nomad.body: A 6-month visa for remote workers with a minimum income threshold and private health insurance.

move.headline: Work or specialist visa
move.body: Usually needs employer sponsorship (e.g. Engineer/Specialist or Highly Skilled Professional). PR possible after years of residence.

destinations.photo: Cape Town · Table Mountain over the Atlantic seaboard

honest.trip: Spectacular scenery and great value, but loadshedding (power cuts) and safety awareness in certain areas need planning around.
honest.nomad: A well-established nomad base with stunning surrounds and fast fibre internet — backup power and area choice matter more than elsewhere.
honest.move: Affordable and beautiful, with a path to residency, though crime concerns and the rand's volatility are real considerations to weigh.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU & CA passports enter visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days.

nomad.headline: Remote Work Visa
nomad.body: A dedicated visa for remote workers earning above a foreign-income threshold, valid up to 3 years.

move.headline: Critical skills / residency visa
move.body: Skilled workers can apply via the critical skills list; financially independent applicants have a separate route to residency.

honest.trip: Slick, safe and easy to navigate, but it's pricier than people expect and the summer heat is genuinely brutal.
honest.nomad: Tax-free income and a polished remote-work visa make this attractive — though it's an expensive base with a car-dependent layout.
honest.move: Modern infrastructure and zero income tax, but residency is employment/sponsorship-tied and the cultural and legal norms differ sharply from the West.

trip.headline: Visa on arrival, up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU, CA & AU passports get a free visa on arrival for tourism, often extendable.

nomad.headline: Virtual Working Programme
nomad.body: A 1-year remote-work visa for employees and freelancers earning above a minimum monthly income.

move.headline: Employment or Golden Visa
move.body: Most residency is employer-sponsored; high earners, investors and specialists can qualify for a long-term Golden Visa.

destinations.photo: Toronto · CN Tower over the harbourfront

honest.trip: Clean, friendly and easy to get around, but accommodation is pricier than most US cities and winters are long and cold.
honest.nomad: Solid infrastructure and a real tech scene, but there's no dedicated nomad visa and the cost of living rivals major US cities.
honest.move: One of the easier Western countries to build a long-term path in, with strong public services — but housing costs and winters are a real adjustment.

trip.headline: eTA or visa-free, up to 6 months
trip.body: Visa-exempt nationals get an eTA on arrival by air; entry is typically granted for up to 6 months.

nomad.headline: Tourist entry covers it
nomad.body: No dedicated nomad visa yet, but the standard 6-month tourist entry comfortably covers most nomad stints.

move.headline: Express Entry / PR pathways
move.body: Skilled-worker immigration via Express Entry or provincial nominee programs leads directly to permanent residency.

honest.trip: Stunning beaches and an easy-going pace, but flights in are long and it's one of the more expensive stops on this list.
honest.nomad: Great weather and lifestyle, but the cost of living is high and there's no nomad-specific visa — most rely on the working holiday route.
honest.move: High quality of life and a clear skilled-migration pathway, though it's a lengthy and competitive points-based process.

trip.headline: eVisitor or ETA, up to 90 days
trip.body: Most EU passports get a free eVisitor visa; US, CA & others get an ETA — both typically valid for 90-day stays.

nomad.headline: Working Holiday visa
nomad.body: For eligible passports aged 18–35 (or 18–30), allowing up to 12 months of work and travel.

move.headline: Skilled migration (points-tested)
move.body: A points-based system assessing age, skills and English ability; successful applicants get permanent residency directly.

destinations.photo: Singapore · Marina Bay skyline at night

honest.trip: Spotless, safe and effortless to navigate, but it's genuinely one of the most expensive cities in the world to even pass through.
honest.nomad: World-class infrastructure and connectivity, but the cost of living is brutal and there's no real nomad visa — most stay on tourist entry.
honest.move: Excellent healthcare, safety and schools, but residency is tightly controlled and almost always requires employer sponsorship.

trip.headline: Visa-free up to 90 days
trip.body: Most US, UK, EU, CA & AU passports enter visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days.

nomad.headline: Tourist entry covers it
nomad.body: No dedicated nomad visa; most remote workers base here on the standard 90-day visa-free entry.

move.headline: Employment Pass
move.body: Skilled professionals need employer sponsorship for an Employment Pass; PR is discretionary and highly selective.

schools.residencyPathway: D4 student visa can convert to a work residency permit (D2/D3); generally leads to permanent residency after 5 years of legal residence.
Student visa can convert to a Temporary Resident work visa with a local job offer; typically leads to Permanent Residency after around 4 years.
No automatic post-study route — graduates generally need to switch to a Non-B work visa with a Thai employer; permanent residency is quota-limited and uncommon.
Study residence permit can convert to a work residence permit; Georgia offers one of the more accessible long-term residency tracks in the region.
18-month post-study job-seeker visa after graduation; once employed, the EU Blue Card route can lead to permanent settlement in as little as 21-33 months.
Student visa can transition to temporary residency with a job or income; typically leads to permanent residency after about 2 years of legal residence.
Graduates can switch to a job-hunting "Designated Activities" visa for up to a year, then a work visa; permanent residency generally requires 5-10 years depending on points earned.
Study visa can convert to a general or critical-skills work visa; permanent residency is typically available after about 5 years on a qualifying work visa.
No direct citizenship/PR route — graduates usually move to employer-sponsored work residency; standout students may qualify for Golden Visa consideration.
Post-Graduation Work Permit for up to 3 years; one of the clearest pathways to Permanent Residency via Express Entry / Canadian Experience Class.
Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) for 2-4 years after study; can lead to permanent residency through skilled-visa streams (subclass 189/190).
Student's Pass holders can apply for a work pass after graduation; permanent residency is discretionary and usually requires several years of employment.
